title: Almost half
hookLine: almost half of a day runs on habit, and Marcus Aurelius says the soul is dyed by what we repeat
carry: the soul is dyed by what we repeat

cards: Which hand held the toothbrush this morning? Which shoe went on first? At the end of the street, did you decide to turn, or did your feet just go?
Most of those are hard to answer, and that's the interesting part. A lot of a day happens without anyone choosing it. A new stretch of the path starts here: habit.
The attention days asked where the mind goes. The habit days ask what the body and the day do while the mind is somewhere else. And the first finding is a simple, startling fraction.

teach.b: First, the diary. Psychologist Wendy Wood and her colleagues asked people to stop at regular times through the day and write down what they were doing, thinking and feeling.
Not a survey about habits: just a running log of ordinary life.
Second, how they spotted a habit: actions done nearly every day, and usually in the same place. Brushing teeth in the same bathroom. Checking the same screen at the same desk.
Third, the fraction. A little under half of what people did in a day fit that pattern. Almost half.
Not most of life, but close enough to make anyone look twice at an ordinary day.
Fourth, where the mind went. During those habits, people often reported thinking about something else entirely. The hands ran the routine; the mind was off planning, worrying, replaying.
So almost half of a day may run on tracks laid down earlier. That can sound like bad news. It can also be good news, because tracks can be laid on purpose.

Long before any diary study, the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote in his Meditations: "Such as are thy habitual thoughts, such also will be the character of thy mind; for the soul is dyed by the thoughts."
Dyed, like cloth soaking in a vat, a little deeper each time. The science measured actions; Marcus was writing about thoughts. Both point at the same quiet power of repetition.

how: People who study their own habits sometimes keep a simple log for a day, noting what they do and where, to see how much of the day runs on routine; contemplatives in several traditions treat repeated thoughts and acts as what slowly shapes a life.

practice: Let the breath settle, then rewind the day so far, slowly, like a video.
Find three things you did without deciding to, the way you made the coffee, the route you took, the first app you opened, and name each one quietly, no judgment, good habit or bad.
Then let them go and rest on the breath, which runs all day without any deciding at all.
